Science · Unit: The Human Body

The Five Senses

A field guide to how your body reads the world. Explore each organ, learn the English vocabulary, and test what you remember.

Organ: The Eye

Sight

Click a number or word to see its meaning here.

The Path of Light

Your eyes collect light and turn it into pictures your brain can understand. Let's follow the path of light through the eye.

First, light enters through the cornea, a clear window that bends the light and starts to focus it. Next, light passes through the pupil, the small opening controlled by the iris. In bright light the pupil gets smaller; in the dark it gets bigger.

The light then travels through the lens, which changes shape to focus objects that are close or far away. It reaches the retina, at the back of the eye, where special cells change light into electrical signals.

Finally, the optic nerve carries these signals to the brain, which creates the image you see. The sclera, the white part of the eye, does not focus light — it simply protects the delicate parts inside.

Check your understanding

1. What controls the size of the pupil?
2. Which part changes light into electrical signals?
3. What is the main job of the cornea?
Did you know? The image that forms on your retina is upside down. Your brain flips it so the world looks right side up.

Common Eye Conditions

  • Myopia (nearsightedness): The eyeball is too long or the cornea is too curved. Distant objects look blurry because light focuses in front of the retina.
  • Hyperopia (farsightedness): The eyeball is too short. Close objects look blurry because light focuses behind the retina.
  • Astigmatism: The cornea or lens has an irregular curve, causing blurred vision at any distance.
  • Cataracts: The lens becomes cloudy and opaque, making vision foggy. Common in older adults.
  • Glaucoma: High pressure inside the eye damages the optic nerve. If untreated, it can cause permanent vision loss.
  • Conjunctivitis (pink eye): Inflammation or infection of the conjunctiva, causing redness, itching, and discharge.

How to Take Care of Your Eyes

  • Wear sunglasses that block UV rays when you are outdoors.
  • Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
  • Eat foods rich in vitamin A (carrots, sweet potatoes) and omega-3 fatty acids (fish).
  • Keep a safe distance from screens and books.
  • Schedule regular eye exams, even if your vision seems fine.
Organ: The Ear

Hearing

Click a number or word to see its meaning here.

The Path of Sound

Every sound starts as a vibration in the air called a sound wave. Your ear collects these waves and turns them into information your brain can understand.

First, the pinna collects sound waves and sends them into the ear canal. The waves travel to the eardrum, a thin membrane, and make it vibrate.

These vibrations move three tiny bones called the ossicles. They amplify the vibrations and pass them to the cochlea, a spiral organ filled with liquid, where tiny hair cells turn the vibrations into electrical signals.

Finally, the auditory nerve carries these signals to the brain, which interprets them as sound — music, voices, or noise.

Check your understanding

1. What happens to the eardrum when sound waves arrive?
2. What is the job of the ossicles?
3. Which part changes vibrations into electrical signals?
Did you know? The stirrup, one of the ossicles, is the smallest bone in your whole body — smaller than a grain of rice.

Common Ear Conditions

  • Tinnitus: A constant ringing, buzzing, or hissing sound in the ears with no external source. Often caused by loud noise exposure.
  • Presbycusis: Age-related hearing loss that gradually reduces the ability to hear high-pitched sounds.
  • Otitis media: An infection of the middle ear, common in children, that causes pain and fluid buildup behind the eardrum.
  • Ménière's disease: A disorder of the inner ear that causes vertigo (spinning sensation), tinnitus, and hearing loss.
  • Noise-induced hearing loss: Damage to the hair cells in the cochlea caused by prolonged exposure to loud sounds. It is permanent and cannot be reversed.

How to Take Care of Your Ears

  • Keep volume below 60% when using headphones or earbuds.
  • Wear earplugs in loud environments (concerts, construction sites).
  • Keep ears dry after swimming to prevent infections.
  • Never insert cotton swabs or sharp objects into the ear canal.
  • Get your hearing checked regularly, especially if you work around loud noise.
Organ: The Nose

Smell

Click a number or word to see its meaning here.

The Path of Smell

Every smell begins with tiny molecules floating in the air. When you breathe in, these molecules enter your nose through the nostrils and travel into the nasal cavity.

At the top of the nasal cavity, millions of olfactory receptors detect the smell molecules. They send signals to the olfactory bulb, a small structure just above the nasal cavity.

The olfactory nerve carries these signals from the bulb directly to the brain, which compares them with smells you already know and identifies the smell — coffee, flowers, or rain.

Check your understanding

1. Where do smell molecules first enter your body?
2. What do olfactory receptors do?
3. What carries smell signals to the brain?
Did you know? Smell is closely connected to memory. That is why a smell can suddenly remind you of a place or a person.

Common Nose & Smell Conditions

  • Anosmia: Complete loss of the sense of smell. It can be caused by viral infections (like COVID-19), head injuries, or neurological conditions.
  • Hyposmia: A reduced ability to detect smells. It may be temporary (from a cold) or permanent.
  • Parosmia: Smells are distorted — something pleasant may smell foul. Often occurs during recovery from anosmia.
  • Rhinitis: Inflammation of the nasal lining, causing a runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, and reduced smell. Can be allergic or non-allergic.
  • Sinusitis: Inflammation or infection of the sinuses (air-filled cavities around the nose), causing pain, pressure, and temporary loss of smell.

How to Take Care of Your Nose & Smell

  • Blow your nose gently, one nostril at a time, to avoid pushing mucus into the sinuses.
  • Use a saline rinse to keep nasal passages clean and moist.
  • Avoid smoking and strong chemical irritants that damage olfactory receptors.
  • Use a humidifier in dry environments to prevent nasal dryness.
  • If you lose your sense of smell suddenly, see a doctor — early treatment improves recovery.
Organ: The Tongue

Taste

Click a number or word to see its meaning here.

The Path of Taste

When you eat, saliva dissolves tiny chemicals from your food. Only dissolved chemicals can be tasted. They touch the papillae, the small bumps you can see on your tongue.

Inside the papillae are taste buds, and each taste bud contains many taste cells. Taste cells react to five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (a savory taste).

When a taste cell detects a flavor, it sends a signal through the gustatory nerve to the brain, which identifies the taste and combines it with smell to create flavor.

Check your understanding

1. What must happen to food chemicals before you can taste them?
2. Where are taste buds located?
3. Which of these is NOT one of the five basic tastes?
Did you know? Flavor is a mix of taste AND smell. That is why food tastes different when you have a cold and your nose is blocked.

Common Taste Conditions

  • Ageusia: Complete loss of taste. It often occurs alongside anosmia (loss of smell) because flavor depends on both senses.
  • Hypogeusia: A reduced ability to taste. Certain flavors (especially salty and sweet) may become harder to detect.
  • Dysgeusia: A distorted sense of taste. Food may taste metallic, salty, or foul even when it is fresh.
  • Burning mouth syndrome: A painful sensation of burning on the tongue and roof of the mouth, often without a visible cause. It can be chronic and stressful.
  • Geographic tongue: Smooth, red patches with white borders appear on the tongue. It is harmless but can cause sensitivity to certain foods.

How to Take Care of Your Tongue & Taste

  • Maintain good oral hygiene: brush your tongue gently along with your teeth.
  • Stay well hydrated — saliva is essential for dissolving food chemicals so you can taste them.
  • Eat a balanced diet with enough vitamin B12 and zinc, which support taste cell health.
  • Avoid extremely hot food or drinks that can damage taste buds.
  • If you notice a persistent change in taste, consult a doctor — it may signal an infection or medication side effect.
Organ: The Skin

Touch

Click a number or word to see its meaning here.

The Path of Touch

Your skin is the largest organ of your body, and it is full of sensory receptors that let you feel the world around you. The outer layer, the epidermis, protects your body, but most receptors are found in the layer below it, the dermis.

The dermis contains sensory receptors, hair follicles, and sweat glands. When a receptor is activated — for example, when you touch something hot — it sends a signal through a nerve to the spinal cord and then to the brain, which interprets it as a specific sensation.

Below the dermis is the hypodermis, a layer of fat that stores energy and cushions the body.

Check your understanding

1. Which layer of skin contains most sensory receptors?
2. What do sensory receptors in the skin detect?
3. What is the deepest layer of the skin called?
Did you know? Your fingertips and lips have many more receptors than your back. That is why they are much more sensitive to touch.

Common Skin & Touch Conditions

  • Dermatitis: General term for skin inflammation. It causes redness, itching, and sometimes blisters. Contact dermatitis is triggered by irritants or allergens.
  • Eczema (atopic dermatitis): A chronic condition that causes dry, itchy, inflamed skin. It often starts in childhood and can flare up periodically.
  • Psoriasis: An autoimmune condition where skin cells grow too fast, forming thick, silvery scales. It can be painful and affect quality of life.
  • Peripheral neuropathy: Damage to peripheral nerves causes numbness, tingling, or burning pain, usually in the hands and feet. Common in diabetes.
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve in the wrist. Causes tingling, numbness, and weakness in the hand and fingers.

How to Take Care of Your Skin & Touch

  • Moisturize your skin daily to prevent dryness and cracking.
  • Apply sunscreen (SPF 30+) every day to protect against UV damage and skin cancer.
  • Check your skin regularly for new moles or changes in existing ones.
  • Wear gloves when handling harsh chemicals or in extreme cold.
  • Maintain good posture and take breaks from repetitive hand movements to prevent nerve compression.

Quiz — The Five Senses

Test your knowledge of all five senses. Answer every question, then click Check answers.

Sight

1. What controls the size of the pupil?
The iris controls the size of the pupil, letting more or less light in.
2. Which part changes light into electrical signals?
The retina contains photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) that convert light into electrical signals.
3. What is the main job of the cornea?
The cornea is a clear protective layer that refracts (bends) about 65% of incoming light.

Hearing

4. What happens to the eardrum when sound waves arrive?
The eardrum vibrates when struck by sound waves, passing vibrations to the ossicles.
5. What is the job of the ossicles?
The three ossicles (hammer, anvil, stirrup) amplify and transmit vibrations from the eardrum to the cochlea.
6. Which part changes vibrations into electrical signals?
The cochlea contains tiny hair cells that convert vibrations into electrical signals sent to the brain.

Smell

7. Where do smell molecules first enter your body?
Smell molecules enter the body through the nostrils and travel into the nasal cavity.
8. What do olfactory receptors do?
Olfactory receptors are specialized cells that detect chemical molecules responsible for smells.
9. What carries smell signals to the brain?
The olfactory nerve carries smell signals from the olfactory bulb to the brain.

Taste

10. What must happen to food chemicals before you can taste them?
Only dissolved chemicals can activate taste cells. Saliva breaks down food so taste buds can detect it.
11. Where are taste buds located?
Taste buds are located inside the papillae, the small bumps visible on the tongue surface.
12. Which of these is NOT one of the five basic tastes?
The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. Spicy is a pain sensation, not a taste.

Touch

13. Which layer of skin contains most sensory receptors?
The dermis, the middle layer of skin, contains most of the sensory receptors, hair follicles, and sweat glands.
14. What do sensory receptors in the skin detect?
Skin receptors detect mechanical pressure, temperature changes, and pain signals.
15. What is the deepest layer of the skin called?
The hypodermis is the deepest layer, made mostly of fat that stores energy and cushions the body.
